# dem-3dep

**USGS 3DEP bare-earth elevation for your US map regions, when you choose it**

- **Version recorded:** station
- **Categories:** `navigation-maps`
- **Upstream:** <https://www.usgs.gov/3d-elevation-program>
- **Needs first:** `osm-regions`

## What it does

With `hammunition station set --dem-source 3dep`, downloads the USGS 3D Elevation Program's 1/3-arc-second (about 10 m) bare-earth tiles covering your US map regions from USGS's own bucket, checks each, and keeps them under /usr/local/share/hammunition/data/dem-3dep/; `dem-qmapshack` then draws QMapShack's hillshade, slope and contours from them instead of from Copernicus. With the default, `copernicus`, it fetches nothing.

## Why you would want it

Copernicus GLO-30, the default, is a surface model: in forest it measures the treetops. Over a forested window in Shenandoah National Park it read 11.8 m above 3DEP on average (measured 2026-09-29), so its contours ride the canopy. 3DEP is the ground, at three times the resolution -- the elevation to want for a trail under trees.

## Before it will work

Map regions set in station config, and `dem_source` set to `3dep`. 3DEP covers the United States and its territories; a region elsewhere gets no 3DEP tile and the plan warns that QMapShack has no elevation for it while 3dep is chosen. Copernicus stays installed either way: BRouter's routing elevation reads it.

## Install and launch

- **Installed with the profile:** [`navigation`](../profiles/navigation.md).
- **Install:** `hammunition install dem-3dep --dry-run`, read the plan, then run it without `--dry-run`.
- **Launch:** Its package ships its own commands and application-menu entry; a unit that ships none gets a generated terminal entry (**D-050**). `hammunition status` lists what is installed.
- **The install needs the network to:** the upstream files the plan lists, each checked against a pinned digest (or, for map and reference data, the publisher or a LAN mirror).

## Offline use

*Not yet documented for this application.* Read “Before it will work” above for what it needs; the install-time network line above is the only offline fact generated from the manifest. Internet, a local network and a radio link are three different things, and this page does not claim any of them works until it says so.

## How it installs

- elevation tiles from usgs-3dep for the regions in station config (Public domain (USGS), https://www.usgs.gov/information-policies-and-instructions/copyrights-and-credits)

## Known problems

About ten times the size of Copernicus: a 3DEP tile is about 480 MB against Copernicus's 46 MB for the same square degree (Shenandoah one tile, Delaware two, about 0.9 GB, Vermont twelve, about 4.4 GB, measured 2026-09-29); the plan prints the size per region before anything downloads. Each tile is checked against the MD5 in the publisher's object metadata (its S3 ETag, carried in the list and asked for again before the download): "MD5 from the publisher's object metadata; not pinned by Hammunition", which catches a damaged download, not a deliberately altered one. Tile names encode latitude and longitude, so they are shown in the plan only. Switching `dem_source` back to `copernicus` removes the 3DEP tiles and redraws the contours from Copernicus on the next install.

## Keeping it current

- probe: none
- strategy: reinstall
- USGS replaces a tile in its current/ folder when new lidar arrives; the weekly check names a carried tile that changed, and the list is regenerated with scripts/gen_3dep_tiles.py --fetch.

## Where to get help with the software itself

The 3D Elevation Program's pages (https://www.usgs.gov/3d-elevation-program) and The National Map's help desk for the data itself.
